items.stem: A RAG assistant serving 5,000 daily support tickets began giving confident, incorrect answers this week. The knowledge corpus was reindexed Monday, and the model provider also rolled out a routine version update the same day. Select two correct first diagnostic steps.

opts.t: Investigate the retrieval pipeline — chunk boundaries, embedding version, and index freshness — for errors traceable to Monday's reindex.
Insert deterministic validation checkpoints between each step of the support pipeline to interrupt any compounding across steps.
Add an instruction to the system prompt directing the assistant to only answer from verified, high-confidence context.
Check the pinned model version against the prior release and run the regression set for the vendor's update.

items.whyRight: Two changes landed the same day, so both must be ruled in or out. The reindex timing points at the retrieval pipeline — chunking, embedding version, index freshness — while the concurrent vendor update requires checking the pinned model version and regression set before either cause is ruled out.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the stem describes a multi-step chain where each step passes its own test yet the combined result is worse; that failure mode is not in evidence here.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction to only use verified context patches the model's output, not the two concurrent changes; it does nothing to check the reindex or the vendor's version update.

items.t1Clause: no multi-step chain is described where each step passes its own test yet the combined result is worse

items.stem: A bank's private-banking unit approves 15 wire transfers a month above $5 million, each requiring a compliance officer's sign-off. A digitization team proposes confidence-tiered auto-approval to modernize the process, auto-approving high-confidence transfers and routing only low-confidence ones to review. What should the team do?

opts.t: Adopt confidence-tiered auto-approval as proposed; it modernizes the workflow and still routes low-confidence transfers to review.
Keep full human review of every transfer regardless of confidence; volume is low, consequence is uniformly high.
Auto-approve all transfers above a set confidence score, and audit a sample of approvals each quarter.
Randomly sample 20% of transfers for compliance review each month, auto-approving the remainder.

items.whyRight: Fifteen high-dollar wire transfers a month is a volume a compliance team can review in full, and every transfer sits above the consequence threshold that requires a human regardless of confidence. Confidence-tiered auto-approval trades that certainty for throughput the volume never demanded in the first place.

whyWrong.A: Confidence-tiered routing is the right move at high volume with mixed consequence, but here every transfer is uniformly high-consequence — the confidence score has nothing to discount.
whyWrong.C: Removing routine review and relying on a quarterly sample abandons oversight on the very population — high-dollar transfers — the sign-off requirement exists to catch.
whyWrong.D: Sampling reviews transfers in proportion to how often they occur, not their consequence, so a costly transfer is no more likely to be the one reviewed.

items.lessonKey: above approve auto confidence even flags high human low past review route severity sla stated threshold window within
items.factAnswerRaw: Human review of every item is correct

items.stem: A payments platform tokenizes cardholder data before it leaves the cardholder-data environment, so downstream services only see tokens. A case-management team investigating a disputed charge needs the real name behind one specific token, for a documented, narrow reason. What should the team add?

opts.t: Re-associate the record's identity locally using the map already held inside the boundary, and log the access.
Let the case-management team query the cardholder-data environment directly for this investigation, bypassing the tokenization layer.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to disclose the real name only for documented case-management requests.
Commission a compliance review of the entire tokenization architecture before allowing any re-identification for this case.

items.whyRight: The boundary already tokenizes correctly, so a narrow, documented need for a specific record's real identity is answered inside that same design: re-associate locally using the identity map the boundary already holds, and log the access. Nothing about a legitimate use case licenses loosening the boundary itself.

whyWrong.B: Bypassing tokenization for this workflow reopens the exposure the boundary exists to prevent; a narrow legitimate need calls for local re-association, not for lifting the boundary.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction is evaluated after the model already holds the real identity, and fits a preference, not this absolute boundary requirement.
whyWrong.D: A full architecture review answers a broader question than this request and delays a narrow, already-scoped need without changing whether the tokenization boundary itself is sound.

items.t1Clause: tokenizes cardholder data before it leaves the cardholder-data environment
items.lessonKey: bound exception infrastructure layer logged named only permitting records region scoped time
items.factAnswerRaw: Re-associate the record's identity locally using the map already held inside the boundary, and log the access.

items.stem: To meet a compliance deadline without building new logging, an audit lead proposes having the model generate a short explanation attached to every declined application, to serve as the audit record for regulators. What is the correct next step?

opts.t: Provide the generated explanation to declined applicants for their own understanding, and file it as the audit record too.
Keep the generated explanation as the audit record, and add a disclaimer noting it may not be fully accurate.
Commission an independent model audit to certify the explanation generator's overall reliability before regulators review any decisions.
Remove the generated explanation as the audit record, and log the inputs, evidence, versions, and threshold behind each decision.

items.whyRight: A generated rationale is confidently wrong about its own causes exactly when it matters most, so it cannot serve as evidence of what happened. Removing it from the audit role and logging the inputs, evidence, versions, and threshold that actually produced each decision reconstructs the real path regulators need.

whyWrong.A: Handing the explanation to applicants is fine, but filing that same generated text as the regulator's audit record is what the section rules out.
whyWrong.B: A disclaimer describes the record's limits without changing what it is; the audit still rests on text produced after the fact, not a trace of what happened.
whyWrong.C: Certifying the generator's general reliability answers a different question than what determined this specific decision, and the compliance deadline does not allow time for an independent audit anyway.

items.t1Clause: to serve as the audit record for regulators

items.stem: An internal reporting agent holds a tool that can permanently delete customer records, though its stated task is read-only summarization. The security lead added invocation logging and asks whether that satisfies the least-privilege requirement before sign-off.

opts.t: Confirm the existing invocation logging and monthly audit review satisfy the least-privilege requirement.
Require a second engineer's sign-off before each delete-tool invocation executes.
Move the delete tool to a scoped service account with tighter database permissions and continuous monitoring.
Remove the delete tool from the agent's tool definitions, since the task does not need it.

items.whyRight: Least privilege is satisfied by removing a capability the task does not need, not by monitoring its use. Deleting the delete tool eliminates the failure class entirely, while logging, sign-off, and scoped permissions only detect or narrow a capability that should not exist.

whyWrong.A: Logging and periodic audit review record misuse after it happens; they do not stop the deletion from executing, which is the audit misconception this section corrects.
whyWrong.B: A second-engineer sign-off is a partial gate that still leaves the delete capability available and depends on whoever grants the approval.
whyWrong.C: A scoped service account and tighter permissions still preserve a delete capability the task never required; thorough permissioning is not the same as removing it.

items.t1Clause: holds a tool that can permanently delete customer records, though its stated task is read-only summarization

items.stem: A federal agency's FedRAMP authorization confines every workload to its approved environment. A project drafting marketing copy from public press releases, touching no protected data, faces a six-week queue to enter that environment, and the program office asks how to proceed.

opts.t: Grant a scoped, reviewed exception for this specific low-risk workload, leaving the general authorized-environment requirement intact.
Relax the authorized-environment requirement generally so future public-data workloads can bypass the queue without individual review.
Require the marketing project to wait in the standard authorization queue like every other workload, regardless of content.
Let the model classify each output as public or sensitive, routing sensitive content to the authorized environment.

items.whyRight: FedRAMP authorization is a property of the environment itself, not something an individual workload can be exempted around. Waiting in the standard queue routes this project through the authorized environment exactly like every other workload — the compliance path section 5.4 actually describes, not a scoped exception that was never part of the mechanism.

whyWrong.A: A scoped exception sounds like a proportionate, risk-based compromise, but authorization is a property of the environment; no exception process, however narrow, confers it on a workload that has not gone through the authorized path.
whyWrong.B: Relaxing the requirement generally reopens the boundary for future workloads that may not stay public, undoing the protection the authorization exists to provide.
whyWrong.D: A model-side classifier is probabilistic; whenever it misclassifies, content would bypass the authorized environment the requirement exists to enforce.

items.t1Clause: confines every workload to its approved environment
items.lessonKey: authorized environment exception general grant intact leaving low requirement reviewed risk scoped specific workload
items.factAnswerRaw: The model is unavailable for that data; route through an authorised environment or keep the data out
